paperTitle: Disentangling the Formation Channels of Pulsars: A Multi-Messenger Approach to Core-Collapse, Electron-Capture, and Accretion-Induced Collapse Origins
paperAbstract: Pulsars—rapidly rotating, magnetized neutron stars—form through multiple astrophysical channels, but the relative contribution of each channel remains uncertain. We propose a systematic framework to disentangle three competing formation pathways: (1) iron core-collapse supernovae (CC-SNe) of massive stars, (2) electron-capture supernovae (EC-SNe) of super-AGB stars, and (3) accretion-induced collapse (AIC) of white dwarfs in binary systems. Each channel predicts distinct signatures in natal kick velocity, spin period, magnetic field strength, binary orbital parameters, and nucleosynthetic yields. By combining pulsar timing surveys, proper motion measurements, gravitational-wave detections, and transient surveys, we will construct a hierarchical Bayesian mixture model that assigns formation-channel probabilities to the observed pulsar population. This approach will quantify the fraction of pulsars born through each channel and test specific predictions about the progenitor mass ranges, kick velocity distributions, and binary survival rates associated with each formation mechanism.
problemStatement: Despite decades of pulsar observations, the relative importance of the three proposed formation channels—iron core-collapse supernovae, electron-capture supernovae, and accretion-induced collapse—remains poorly constrained. Young pulsar populations are broadly consistent with CC-SNe, but the existence of low-kick neutron stars in wide binaries (e.g., the double pulsar PSR J0737-3039A/B) and the potential for AIC to produce magnetars indicate that additional channels contribute. No existing study has simultaneously modeled all three channels with a unified statistical framework that accounts for observational selection effects, making it impossible to robustly quantify each channel's contribution to the Galactic pulsar population.
hypothesis: Pulsars form through three physically distinct channels—iron CC-SNe, EC-SNe, and AIC—each producing neutron stars with statistically distinguishable distributions of natal kick velocity (v_kick), surface magnetic field (B), spin period at birth (P₀), and binary orbital eccentricity (e). Specifically: (H1) CC-SNe produce the majority (~80%) of isolated young pulsars with v_kick > 200 km/s and B > 10¹² G; (H2) EC-SNe produce ~15% of pulsars, preferentially in wide binaries with v_kick < 100 km/s and e < 0.1; (H3) AIC produces ~5% of pulsars, predominantly millisecond pulsars and magnetars with B > 10¹⁴ G. If the observed pulsar population cannot be decomposed into three statistically distinct sub-populations with properties matching these predictions, the multi-channel hypothesis is falsified.
rationale: Theoretical work on core-collapse supernovae establishes that iron CC-SNe of massive stars (M ≳ 8–10 M☉) are the dominant neutron star formation channel, producing pulsars with high kick velocities and strong magnetic fields (Cerdá-Durán & Elias-Rosa 2018; Janka 2004). However, the discovery of wide binary pulsars with low eccentricities and small space velocities—most notably the double pulsar PSR J0737-3039A/B (Ferdman et al. 2013)—indicates that a subset of neutron stars formed through a lower-energy channel. Electron-capture supernovae of super-AGB stars provide a natural explanation: these events have smaller ejecta masses and are predicted to impart smaller natal kicks (Wang et al. 2025; Pan et al. 2022). Meanwhile, recent GRMHD simulations demonstrate that accretion-induced collapse of magnetized white dwarfs can produce neutron star remnants with magnetar-strength fields (Micchi et al. 2026), and population synthesis shows that both CC-SNe and AIC can contribute to the millisecond pulsar population (Zhu et al. 2015). The predicted observable signatures—kick velocity, magnetic field, spin period, and binary eccentricity—differ systematically across channels, enabling statistical decomposition of the observed pulsar population.
technicalDetails: We will construct a hierarchical Bayesian mixture model with three components corresponding to the CC-SN, EC-SN, and AIC formation channels. For each channel, we define parametric prior distributions on the key observables: (i) natal kick velocity v_kick drawn from a Maxwellian with channel-specific dispersion σ_v; (ii) surface dipole magnetic field log₁₀(B/G) drawn from a Gaussian with channel-specific mean and variance; (iii) birth spin period P₀ drawn from a log-normal distribution; (iv) orbital eccentricity e drawn from a Beta distribution for binary pulsars. The mixture weights (w_CC, w_EC, w_AIC) are free parameters constrained to sum to unity. We incorporate a selection function that accounts for radio survey sensitivity (flux density limits, dispersion measure biases, scintillation) and gravitational-wave detector sensitivity to avoid observational biases. The model will be fit to a catalog of ~3,500 known radio pulsars with measured periods, period derivatives, proper motions, and binary parameters, supplemented by LIGO/Virgo neutron star merger events and transient survey upper limits on AIC rates.
methods: 1. Catalog compilation: Assemble a homogeneous catalog of radio pulsars from ATNF, PALFA, HTRU, and MeerKAT surveys with measured P, Ṗ, DM, proper motion (where available), and binary orbital parameters. Apply consistent selection criteria and correct for the Shklovskii effect and acceleration biases. 2. Channel prior calibration: Use stellar evolution models (MESA) to derive predicted distributions of neutron star birth properties for each channel: CC-SNe from pre-supernova progenitor models (M = 8–25 M☉), EC-SNe from super-AGB models (M = 8–10 M☉), and AIC from binary white dwarf evolution calculations. 3. Selection function modeling: Implement a pulsar survey simulator that maps intrinsic pulsar properties to detection probabilities given survey sensitivity, sky position, DM, and scattering. 4. Hierarchical Bayesian inference: Use nested sampling (dynesty/MultiNest) to infer the mixture weights and channel-specific hyperparameters. 5. Cross-validation: Compare model predictions against independent observables not used in fitting: Galactic supernova rate, local pulsar birth rate from OB associations, and gravitational-wave merger rate.

experiments.design: We perform a series of increasingly complex model comparisons to test the multi-channel hypothesis. Experiment 1: Fit a single-channel model (CC-SN only) to the full pulsar catalog and quantify the residuals in kick velocity and eccentricity distributions. Experiment 2: Fit a two-channel model (CC-SN + EC-SN) and assess whether the addition of an EC-SN component significantly improves the fit via Bayesian evidence ratios. Experiment 3: Fit the full three-channel model (CC-SN + EC-SN + AIC) and determine whether AIC is required by the data. Experiment 4: Perform leave-one-out cross-validation by withholding the double pulsar system and low-eccentricity wide binaries, then predicting their properties from the remaining data. Experiment 5: Compare predicted AIC transient rates against upper limits from optical transient surveys (ZTF, ATLAS) and radio surveys.
baselines: Single-channel CC-SN model (standard assumption in pulsar population synthesis)
Two-channel model (CC-SN + EC-SN) without AIC component
Non-parametric kernel density estimate of pulsar property distributions (no channel assumption)
Previous population synthesis results from binary population synthesis codes (StarTrack, COMPAS)
metrics: Bayesian evidence (log Z) for model comparison between 1-, 2-, and 3-channel models
Posterior distributions on mixture weights (w_CC, w_EC, w_AIC) with credible intervals
Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics comparing predicted vs observed kick velocity distributions
Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics comparing predicted vs observed eccentricity distributions for binary pulsars
Predicted vs observed ratio of millisecond pulsars to normal pulsars
Predicted AIC transient rate compared to observational upper limits

datasets.source: ATNF Pulsar Catalog (v1.68+), supplemented by discoveries from PALFA, HTRU, MeerKAT TRAPUM, and CHIME/FRB pulsar surveys. Proper motion measurements from pulsar timing arrays (e.g., NANOGrav, PPTA). Gravitational-wave event catalog from LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA (O1–O4). Optical transient survey upper limits from ZTF and ATLAS.
datasets.target: Posterior distributions on formation-channel mixture weights and channel-specific hyperparameters (kick velocity dispersion, magnetic field distribution, spin period distribution) for the Galactic pulsar population. Predicted formation rate of each channel in units of events per century per Milky Way-like galaxy.

results: We expect the three-channel model to be strongly favored over single- and two-channel alternatives based on Bayesian evidence. Specifically: (1) The CC-SN channel will dominate with w_CC ≈ 0.75–0.85, consistent with the high kick velocities observed for young pulsars. (2) The EC-SN channel will contribute w_EC ≈ 0.10–0.20, primarily accounting for low-eccentricity wide binary pulsars and neutron stars with low space velocities. (3) The AIC channel will contribute w_AIC ≈ 0.03–0.08, predominantly producing millisecond pulsars and a subset of magnetars. If the data instead favor a two-channel model without AIC, this would falsify the hypothesis that AIC is a significant pulsar formation channel. If the three-channel model fails to reproduce the observed eccentricity distribution of binary pulsars, this would indicate that additional physics (e.g., common-envelope evolution effects on orbital circularization) must be incorporated. The predicted AIC transient rate will be compared against observational upper limits; a predicted rate below current detection thresholds would motivate dedicated high-cadence transient surveys targeting AIC candidates.
